readerTitle: You loved the sauce. Do you remember who made it?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소스 제조사·슈퍼마켓, 산업용 컴프레서 제조사·유통사) + 실제 관찰 (대형 유통사와 온라인 마켓플레이스의 자체 브랜드 판매)
insight: 제품이 충성을 얻어도, 고객의 이름과 연락 경로를 쥔 쪽이 그 충성을 가져간다.
misconception: 좋은 제품이 잘 팔리고 있으면 고객은 이미 우리 고객이다. 유통 채널은 물건을 옮겨 줄 뿐이다.

sources.text: 대형 유통사와 온라인 마켓플레이스가 입점 브랜드 옆에서 자체 브랜드(PB) 상품을 판매하는 일반적 관행 (실제 관찰)
소스 제조사, 컴프레서 제조사 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 5번 카드의 '많은 대형 유통사와 마켓플레이스가 자체 브랜드를 입점 브랜드 옆에서 팔고, 두 쪽의 판매 데이터를 모두 본다'는 일반적 관찰입니다. 특정 기업명이나 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 데이터 활용 범위는 회사와 국가 규제에 따라 다르므로 단정하지 않도록 문구를 확인하세요.
softwareNote의 앱스토어·마켓플레이스가 고객 이메일과 결제를 쥔다는 설명은 플랫폼마다 정책이 다릅니다. '자주(often)'로 완화해 썼습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
6번 카드의 고객 연락처 수집 시 동의(permission) 언급은 일반 원칙으로만 다루며, 특정 국가의 개인정보 법률 조언은 하지 않습니다.

cards.title: You loved the sauce. Do you remember who made it?
body: You find a great chili sauce at your supermarket. You buy a bottle every week for a year.
Then one day it's gone. A cheaper store-brand bottle sits in its place. You shrug and buy that instead.
The maker never knew your name. So they had no way to tell you where to find them.

image.label: Empty shelf gap next to a store-brand chili sauce bottle
image.brief: 슈퍼마켓 소스 진열대 클로즈업. 한 칸이 비어 있고 'Sold out' 대신 그 자리에 무지 라벨의 매장 자체 브랜드 병이 놓여 있음. 쇼핑객이 별생각 없이 그 병을 집는 손. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Now you're the sauce maker.
body: Your sauce sells in 40 supermarkets, and sales are growing. You have a small budget for one project this year.

options.text: Pay for end-of-aisle displays in more stores
options.feedback: You'll likely sell more this quarter. But every new fan is still the store's customer, not yours. If the shelf goes, so do they.

options.text: Add a recipe club to the label: scan to join, get recipes and refill offers
options.feedback: Slower and smaller at first. But you start learning who your fans are, and you can reach them without asking the store.

options.text: Open a web shop priced below the supermarkets
options.feedback: You may win some direct buyers, but the stores see you undercutting them and may drop you. You could trade 40 shelves for a website few people visit.

cards.title: The store knew more than you did.
body: The supermarket's loyalty card showed who bought your sauce, how often, and what else went in their basket.
With that, it could launch its own version, place it next to yours, and send coupons to your best buyers. You saw only one number: cases ordered.
Your product **earned** the loyalty. The store **owned** it.

cards.title: Owning the customer
body: **Owning the customer** means holding the direct relationship: you know who buys, you can reach them again, and they come back to you by name. Three quick tests:
list: Do you know who they are?
Can you reach them without paying someone in between?
If your product vanished from the shelf, would they come looking for *you*?
cards.callout: Three yeses mean you own the customer. Three noes mean you rent access from someone who does.
cards.softwareNote: An app sold through an app store, or a tool listed on a marketplace, faces the same question. The platform often holds the payment, the email and the reviews. Who can send the customer a message tomorrow?

cards.title: Whoever owns the customer sets the terms.
body: A business that sells only through others rents its access to customers. Rent can rise: higher fees, worse shelf spots, demands to fund promotions.
A business with its own line to customers has a fallback. If one channel drops it, it can still tell buyers where to go next. That makes it a stronger negotiator, too.
This is no secret to the middle. Many large retailers and online marketplaces sell their own-brand goods next to the brands they carry, and they see the sales of both.

cards.title: Don't fight the channel that feeds you.
body: Owning the customer costs money and effort. Someone has to answer emails, ship refills and keep the list useful.
The bigger risk is channel conflict. If your direct offer undercuts your retailers or distributors, they may drop you before your own channel can replace them.

The safer path is a direct link that adds something the channel doesn't: recipes, warranty, service reminders. And ask customers for permission to stay in touch. A list built by trickery isn't a relationship.

cards.title: Now it's a factory.
body: You make industrial air compressors. Distributors sell and service them for factories across the country. You don't know which factories use your machines.
A rival has just signed your biggest distributor. What's your best move?

options.text: Cut out distributors and build your own national sales team
options.feedback: You'd own every customer, but the cost is huge and your other distributors would likely switch brands before your team was ready.

options.text: Launch warranty registration and maintenance reminders, and credit distributors for every parts order
options.feedback: You learn which factories run your machines and give them a reason to know your name. Distributors still earn, so they have little reason to fight it.

options.text: Ask your remaining distributors to share their customer lists
options.feedback: Worth asking, but those lists are their most valuable asset. Most will say no, and the request may make them nervous about you.

cards.softwareNote: In a software product sold through resellers, the same move is product-level contact: in-app onboarding, account registration and update notes that reach the user directly, while resellers keep their margin.

cards.title: Sell through others, but keep a line of your own.
body: Channels can move your product. Only a direct relationship keeps your customers when the channel changes its mind.
**Try it today:** look at your last 20 customers. For how many do you have a name and a way to reach them without paying anyone? That share is the part of your business you truly own.
